title: sycl: FWHT kernels for block widths above 512
body:
## Overview

The SYCL FWHT covers 64 to 512 via the standard butterfly network, plus 384/640/768/1280 via the Kronecker/Paley construction added separately in #28016. Neither path covers the pure power-of-2 widths above 512 that the Hadamard hint can produce (1024, 2048, 4096, 8192); those still fall through to the default case and run as a dense GEMM against the materialized rotation tensor, correct but O(n^2) instead of O(n log n).

fwht_kernel_wide runs one row per work-group instead of per sub-group, so each work-item keeps N/NT values rather than N/WARP_SIZE. Butterflies below the sub-group width still shuffle; those up to the work-group width go through work-group local memory; the rest stay in registers. Same butterfly and sign convention as the existing narrow kernel.

## Additional information

Verification: `test-backend-ops test -b SYCL0 -o MUL_MAT_HADAMARD` passes 26/26 on an Intel Arc B390 (Xe3 iGPU, Windows, oneAPI 2025.3, Level Zero) at the current head, covering every width from 1024 to 16384 with both F32 and F16 src1. Before that I checked the kernel algorithm with a standalone harness on a SYCL CPU device against an independent Hadamard reference; the numbers are in the commit message. The test cases for these widths are already on master from #29095, so this PR only touches the SYCL FWHT.

title: CUDA: tune fp16 tile FlashAttention configs for head sizes 40-112
body:
## Overview
This PR optimizes the FlashAttention FP16 tile configurations for NVIDIA GPUs, addressing the header TODO in `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-tile.cuh` to "optimize kernel parameters for FP16 NVIDIA (P100)" for head sizes 40, 64, 72, 80, 96, and 112. 

By retuning exactly 13 rows in `ggml_cuda_fattn_tile_get_config_nvidia_fp16`, this PR achieves a mean kernel-level speedup of **+14.5% on P100** (up to +31.5%), with **zero regressions** across Pascal (P100), Volta (V100), and Blackwell architectures. 

End-to-end, this yields a solid **+2% decode speedup for phi-2** at short contexts, scaling to **+9.4% at 8K context**, while remaining neutral for other models and prefill workloads.

## Additional information

### 1. Hardware & Methodology

| GPU | cc | driver | toolchain |
|-----|-----|--------|-----------|
| Tesla P100-PCIE/SXM 16GB | 6.0  | 580.x      | CUDA 12.9, g++-14 |
| Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB     | 7.0  | 580.159.03 | CUDA 12.9, g++-14 |
| RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell   | 12.0 | -          | CUDA 12.9         |

**Methodology:**
* Tests were performed via paired alternating A/B runs.
* Execution used `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (because `RUNPATH` would otherwise override).
* GPU persistence mode was ON and clocks were locked.

### 2. Microbenchmark Gains (Isolated Kernel)
Rows were timed via `test-backend-ops perf -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT` (4 heads, KV 4096, F16 K/V, F32 accum). `ncols` maps to the batch size / GQA ratio. 

**Noise Floor:** In-run noise floors were established by the 13 unmodified guard rows at 2.6% for P100 and 1.8% for V100. We define "neutral" as any delta falling within this noise floor. Under this definition, **every modified row is win-or-neutral across all architectures it runs on**.

| hs | ncols | default | tuned | P100 (cc6.0) | V100 (cc7.0) | Blackwell (cc12.0) |
|----|-------|---------|-------|------|------|-----------|
| 40  | 2  | (64,2,64,40)   | (128,3,128,40) | +26.6% | +14.0% | +7.0%  |
| 40  | 4  | (128,2,64,40)  | (128,2,128,40) | +21.3% | +20.9% | +15.2% |
| 40  | 8  | (256,2,64,40)  | (128,3,128,40) | +9.4%  | +24.4% | +5.5%  |
| 64  | 8  | (256,2,64,64)  | (256,3,128,64) | +6.0%  | +9.0%  | n/a*   |
| 72  | 2  | (64,2,64,72)   | (128,2,64,72)  | +4.6%  | +2.7%  | +13.3% |
| 72  | 4  | (128,2,64,72)  | (128,3,128,72) | +24.3% | +14.8% | +21.0% |
| 80  | 2  | (64,2,64,40)   | (128,2,64,40)  | +4.9%  | -0.7%  | n/a*   |
| 80  | 32 | (256,2,64,40)  | (256,2,128,40) | +10.9% | +0.0%  | n/a*   |
| 96  | 32 | (256,2,64,48)  | (256,2,128,24) | +6.8%  | +0.0%  | n/a*   |
| 112 | 2  | (64,2,64,56)   | (128,3,64,56)  | +31.5% | +1.5%  | n/a*   |
| 112 | 8  | (256,2,64,56)  | (256,3,64,112) | +18.5% | +53.9% | n/a*   |
| 112 | 16 | (256,2,64,56)  | (256,2,32,112) | +17.8% | +41.0% | n/a*   |
| 112 | 32 | (256,2,64,56)  | (256,2,128,56) | +5.9%  | +0.0%  | n/a*   |

*(Note: Every tensor-core branch is explicitly guarded by ne[0] != 40 && ne[0] != 72, meaning head sizes 40 and 72 fall through to the TILE kernel on all fast-fp16 NVIDIA GPUs through Blackwell.)*
(**row does not execute on the arch)*

### 3. Tuning Mechanisms
* **`nbatch_fa` 64 -> 128:** Amortizes softmax/rescale overhead by halving the KQ-tile loop iteration count. Main driver for small-ncols rows.
* **`occupancy` 2 -> 3:** Hides more latency with a third resident block per SM, taking advantage of the shared-memory headroom left by small heads.
* **`nthreads` 64 -> 128:** Doubles per-block parallelism at small batch sizes (`ncols=2`), fixing severe SM underutilization.
* **`nbatch_K` full-DV:** Halves K-loop overhead for several rows by loading the full DV per iteration instead of DV/2.

### 4. End-to-End Scaling & Cross-Model Safety (P100)
Tested via `llama-bench`.

**Cross-model Safety:**
Models hitting untuned batch-1 rows showed flat performance within the run-to-run noise margin for both prefill and decode, indicating zero regressions in production scenarios. 

| model | params | head size | decode Δ | prefill Δ |
|-------|--------|-----------|----------|-----------|
| TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat  | 1.1B | 64  | -1.15% (noise) | +0.22% |
| phi-2                | 2.7B | 80  | +2.13%         | -0.14% |
| Phi-3-mini-4k        | 3.8B | 96  | -0.02%         | -0.02% |
| Mistral-7B-Instruct  | 7B   | 128 | -0.02%         | +0.24% |

**Phi-2 (hs 80) Decode Scaling:**
Single-batch decode hits the tuned `80/2` row. The speedup scales effectively with context length as FlashAttention consumes a larger share of the decode step relative to weight-streaming:

| KV depth | base t/s | tuned t/s | decode Δ | sd |
|----------|----------|-----------|----------|------|
| 0    | 82.80 | 83.73 | +1.10% | 2.10 |
| 1024 | 78.45 | 80.36 | +2.44% | 0.75 |
| 2048 | 74.38 | 74.70 | +0.42% | 2.48 |
| 4096 | 67.50 | 70.14 | +3.91% | 0.07 |
| 8192 | 54.91 | 60.08 | +9.41% | 0.14 |

*Caveat: Depth > 2048 exceeds phi-2's native context; these are throughput measurements, not a generation-quality claim.*

### 5. Correctness
Passed `test-backend-ops test -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT`:
* **P100 (cc6.0):** 2880/2880 OK, 0 FAIL.
* **V100 (cc7.0):** 2656/2656 OK, byte-identical against the untuned baseline for affected head sizes. (Note: The full V100 suite throws a `cudaFuncSetAttribute` invalid argument abort on the hs 320/256 MLA test at `fattn-mma-f16.cuh:1945` because it exceeds Volta's 96 KB smem limit. Verified on the baseline(untuned branch) to be identical error, unrelated to this pr.
* **Blackwell (cc12.0):** 2880/2880 OK.

title: graph : do not reuse a token graph as an embedding graph (and vice versa)
body:
`llm_graph_input_embd` and `llm_graph_input_embd_h` pick between the token-lookup branch and the direct-embedding branch when the graph is built. `can_reuse()` only compares tensor shapes, and shapes cannot tell the two apart: an mtmd embedding batch and a token batch can both be 512 rows and still need different graphs.

The inputs now carry which branch they were built for and refuse a cross-modality reuse. This is strictly more conservative than the `true` it replaces — it can only refuse a reuse, never enable a wrong one.

I found this while chasing a scheduler-topology carryover after mtmd decodes, so it is motivated by a real failure rather than by inspection. Being honest about the evidence: I did not isolate a performance delta for this change on its own. It was already in place before I measured the carryover, and the fix that closed that specific regression is the re-reserve in #27428's companion PR. What this change stands on is correctness — today a 512-row embedding batch and a 512-row token batch are indistinguishable to `can_reuse()`, and nothing prevents the wrong graph from being replayed.

Call sites pass `ubatch.token != nullptr`. The parameter defaults to `true`, so models not touched here keep their current behaviour.

Touches `src/llama-graph.h`, `src/llama-graph.cpp` and 11 files under `src/models/`.

title: musa: define __CUDA_ARCH__ and fix the q8_0 and iq4_nl dequantization kernels
body:
## Overview

As discussed in https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29292#issuecomment-5794058932, this is the separate PR that aligns `__CUDA_ARCH__` with the HIP approach.

`__CUDA_ARCH__` is defined in `vendors/hip.h`, but it was never defined for MUSA. Every architecture test in the shared `ggml-cuda` sources therefore evaluated to 0, and the kernels guarded by them were compiled with an empty body and still launched. `dequantize_block_q8_0_f16`, guarded by `__CUDA_ARCH__ >= GGML_CUDA_CC_PASCAL`, was one of them: every `q8_0` dequantization produced garbage.

Two changes in this PR:

- `vendors/musa.h`: define `__CUDA_ARCH__` as `GGML_CUDA_CC_RUBIN` (1300), the way HIP does, and explicitly exclude the NVIDIA-only features that this value would otherwise enable — `TURING_MMA_AVAILABLE`, `AMPERE_MMA_AVAILABLE`, `CP_ASYNC_AVAILABLE`, `__reduce_add_sync`, the Ampere/Pascal-DP4A MMQ and MMVQ configurations and `__bfloat1622float2`. The definition is scoped to the device pass (`#ifdef __MUSA_ARCH__`): CUB tells host from device code with `defined(__CUDA_ARCH__) || defined(__MUSA_ARCH__)` in `cub/util_debug.cuh`, which is also how nvcc behaves.
- `convert.cu`: carry over the `dequantize_block_iq4_nl` short-row guard from #29292 (cherry-picked with `-x`), so that this PR can replace it.

NVIDIA and HIP builds are unaffected: `defined(__MUSA_ARCH__)` is false there, and the added `!defined(GGML_USE_MUSA)` conditions are no-ops. The host pass is unchanged as well — with the definition scoped to the device pass, the feature macros stay undefined for MUSA exactly as before.

## Additional information

Measured with `test-backend-ops` on an MTT S5000 (MUSA SDK 5.2, MUSA architecture `31`, driver 5.2.0-server), single card, built with `-DGGML_MUSA=ON -DGGML_BACKEND_DL=ON -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=ON`:

| build | `test-backend-ops` |
| --- | --- |
| master | 12458/12507 — 49 failures: 31x `MUL_MAT_ID` and 18x `MUL_MAT`, all `type_a=q8_0`, `NaN` or error above tolerance |
| this PR | 12507/12507 |

`MUL_MAT_ID` alone: 899/929 on master, 929/929 here. The failing case is exactly the one that reaches `batched_mul_mat_traits<GGML_TYPE_F16>::convert` for quantized `src0`. CUB-based ops (`ARGSORT`, `TOP_K`, `SUM`, `CUMSUM`, `MEAN`, `SSM_SCAN`) are 682/682, and the same tree also builds for `MUSA_ARCHITECTURES=21;22;31` (only `31` was run on hardware). Model smokes (Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M with `-fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0`, and `llama-bench`) are unchanged to within noise, and the backend capability list for MUSA is byte-identical to master.

The first commit fixes the `q8_0` case; the second one is #29292's other fix, which is backend independent.

## Overview

Fix argsort on HIP and MUSA builds for rows wider than 1024. Without CUB the bitonic kernel launched one thread per padded column, so a 2048 wide argsort aborted with an invalid block configuration. title: speculative : lag the MTP catch-up decode to restore multi-GPU prefill
body:
Fixes #27428.

The MTP catch-up reads the target's hidden rows through `llama_get_embeddings_nextn(ctx_tgt)`. That read forces the target's ubatch to complete before the MTP batch can be built, so on a `--split-mode layer` setup the next device cannot start the following ubatch and the pipeline overlap is lost. A single GPU has no overlap to lose, which is the asymmetry reported in the issue. Generation is unaffected: a generation step is one small batch with no next ubatch to overlap with.

This lets the catch-up lag one logical batch behind the target:

- the target context keeps two pinned host views of the nextn rows, each with a backend event recorded after its async D2H copy. MTP consumes the previous view and waits only on that view's event, never on the decode in flight
- `process()` parks the batch instead of decoding it immediately. Intermediate prompt chunks request no logits, so nothing reads them that turn and they can lag safely. The final prompt chunk and every generation batch do request logits and stay on the synchronous path that sampling correctness needs
- `begin()` and `draft()` flush whatever is parked against the current view before they read

Two supporting changes, both needed for the above to pay off:

- **the MTP context is excluded from pipeline parallelism.** Its single block gains nothing from it, and since the scheduler hands each newly allocated graph the next of its input copies, MTP alternating the catch-up and draft graphs made every draft graph see a new input address and re-record its CUDA graph instead of replaying it
- **the MTP context reserves a K/V-only graph**, since it consumes prompt batches only to populate its K/V and never runs the full-output pass the generic reserve sizes for

One more change rides along, because it is the same scheduler problem seen from the other side: an external mtmd decode moves the output-ring phase and leaves the scheduler in the embedding topology, so `llama_reset_after_external_decode()` forces a re-reserve before the next text batch. Without it, prompt processing in the same process drops by about a third after a few images and stays there until restart.

## Measurements

Two builds of `b29c606` (v0.4.1) differing only by this branch, same machine (2x RTX 3090, `--split-mode layer`, `--tensor-split 0.525,0.475`), Qwen3.8-27B hybrid (arch `qwen35`), `--spec-type draft-mtp`, `--ctx-size 262144`. Identical 10464-token prompt, greedy sampling, `cache_prompt: false` so every round pays the full prefill, 200 tokens generated, 3 rounds per arm.

| | prompt processing | generation |
|---|---|---|
| `b29c606` as released | 1132.0 t/s | 57.98 t/s |
| this branch | **1848.8 t/s** | 59.98 t/s |

Prompt processing is the warm rounds (2 and 3); including the cold first round the figures are 1111.5 and 1779.1 t/s, so +60% rather than +63%. Generation is the mean of all three rounds, with a round-to-round spread of 2.7% and 2.2% respectively — the small gain there is inside that spread, and draft acceptance was 71.4% in both arms, so nothing about generation is being traded away.

A note on measurement, in case it saves someone time: this cannot be benchmarked at a normal sampling temperature. MTP acceptance tracks how predictable the generated text is far more than it tracks any flag, and at `temperature 0.7` the spread *within* one configuration was as wide as the difference between configurations.

## Also fixes a silent startup fallback

On this configuration the released build fails to allocate the MTP draft context's compute buffer on the second device and quietly continues without pipeline parallelism for the rest of the run:

```
ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: allocating 1226.06 MiB on device 1: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory
ggml_gallocr_reserve_n_impl: failed to allocate CUDA1 buffer of size 1285620224
graph_reserve: failed to allocate compute buffers
sched_reserve: compute buffer allocation failed, retrying without pipeline parallelism
```

Excluding the MTP context from pipeline parallelism removes this; the startup log is clean on the branch.

## Notes for reviewers

- The K/V-only graph path is implemented for `qwen35` only; other MTP architectures keep the existing behaviour. The lag itself is architecture-independent.
- A branch with this and the graph-reuse change together, for anyone who wants to build both at once: https://github.com/Nilline/llama.cpp/tree/issue-27428-mtp-prefill

title: ggml-cpu x86: exact -128 handling in int8 dot-product helpers (fix #29351; excludes q1_0, iq2_*, iq3_*, sgemm, repack)
body:
Fixes #29351

## Overview

The `sign_epi8` + `maddubs` trick in the x86 int8 dot-product helpers cannot negate `-128` (negating -128 in int8 stays -128), and `(-128) * (-128) = 16384` has no `u8 x s8` factorization at all, so any block whose y-side contains -128 is silently wrong on non-VNNI builds. llama.cpp's own quantizers clamp to [-127, 127], but -128 is reachable via the public API and hand-built/third-party GGUFs, and it makes generic-C and SIMD builds diverge.

This PR fixes it by making the operand order explicit: the activation (which may contain -128) is always the first argument to the int8 helpers, and the bounded weight is the second. The bug only fires when the sign'd operand is -128 AND the abs'd operand is also -128, which only happens for q8_0 x q8_0 (both sides full range). So:

- All call sites swap operands to put the activation first.
- Only the two q8_0 x q8_0 guarded float paths widen to int16 (pair bound 2*128*127 = 32512 < 2^15).
- The guards are removed from `mul_add_epi8` / `mul_add_epi8_sse` (back to base behavior).

## Additional information

Scope (fixed): q4_0, q5_0, q8_0, mxfp4, nvfp4, iq1_s, iq1_m, iq4_nl, iq4_xs — SSSE3 / AVX / AVX2 / AVX-VNNI / AVX512-VNNI / AVX512-INT8 paths in `ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/x86/quants.c`.

Excluded (unchanged, fail identically on base — structural, not a 2-operand swap): q1_0, iq2_xxs, iq2_xs, iq2_s, iq3_xxs, iq3_s, `llamafile/sgemm.cpp`, `arch/x86/repack.cpp`.

New helpers: `mul_sum_i8_pairs_wide` (shared int16 widening), `mul_sum_i8_pairs_float_guarded` and `mul_sum_i8_quad_float_guarded` (q8_0 x q8_0 only). Operands swapped at the q4_0/q5_0/mxfp4/nvfp4/iq1_s/iq1_m/iq4_nl/iq4_xs call sites; AVX-only float path restored to base.

Diffstat: 2 files, 330 insertions, 49 deletions (`quants.c` 184, `tests/test-quantize-fns.cpp` +195).

Testing:
- Regression test `test_vec_dot_q8_0_i8_min` added to existing `tests/test-quantize-fns.cpp` (no new files). Fails 9/9 on base (native + AVX-only), passes 0/9 on this PR.
- New `test_vec_dot_neg128`: injects a -128 byte into the q8_0/q8_K activation of q4_0, q5_0, mxfp4, nvfp4, iq4_nl, iq1_s, iq1_m, iq4_xs and checks the SIMD vec_dot against the generic reference (rel < 1e-4). Fails on base (rel 0.001-0.047), passes on this PR.

title: qwen4exp's SCALE -> SIGMOID -> SCALE -> hc_post chain as one kernel
body:
The PR is a Vulkan-only fusion that runs qwen4exp's SCALE -> SIGMOID -> SCALE -> hc_post chain as one kernel and stops the reorder pass from splitting it; it gives exact output and +3.8% decode, passes all 18,993 tests.

## Overview

qwen4exp (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) builds each hyper-connection's scatter weights as w = 2*sigmoid(inject/hc): three tiny ops on a 4-element tensor, right before dsv4_hc_post. That happens twice per layer, 96 times per token. On Vulkan, decode is limited by the number of kernel dispatches, not by arithmetic, so those 288 dispatches per token cost real time.

The change, all inside the Vulkan backend:

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
|New fusion HC_POST_GATE|Detects SCALE -> SIGMOID -> SCALE -> DSV4_HC_POST and runs it as one dispatch; hc_post computes the gate while loading post[] into shared memory|
|Match check|Fuses only when the op is sigmoid, neither scale has a bias, the input is f32, and the shapes match; anything else runs unfused|
|Reorder registration |Without it, Vulkan's reorder pass split all 96 chains per token (0 left adjacent), so the fusion could never fire|
|Allocation guard |add_pattern_alloc_deps keeps the input alive through the fused output, so the overlap check doesn't silently cancel the fusion|
| Test|A gated variable on the existing test_dsv4_hc_post; no new test file                                                                             

Checks:

title: Feature - Deterministic Draft Filter with pluggable SDK
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

Introduces a deterministic plugin mechanism via a simple SPI that keeps changes to the core at a minimal. 
This is a generic mechanism however what makes it different from the current per token validation is that it plugs into the existing MTP pipeline, by default the plugin will determine if a token is filtered or not but any valid token will be verified by the target and the bonus token is always generated unless a valid termination completes such as a complete parse if using xgrammar. With the --det-draft-accept-all , only the plugin's logic is used to verify, the target model's verification is bypassed even the correction/bonus token is arbitrated and on low end commodity hardware can result in faster TPS along with the guaranteed verification. 

A working PoC that uses Xgrammar for verifying Java,Python,JavaScript and C is under `deterministic-draft-model-poc` 

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

Feature - Deterministic Draft Filter with pluggable SDK
- Add deterministic draft filter as a new speculative draft type
- Pluggable SDK via dlopen/dlsym with a single C API contract
- XGrammar based POC demonstrating plugin implementation. Bundled grammars for C, Java, Python, JavaScript Grammar format is XGrammar EBNF.
- Incremental draft validation: one persistent matcher per slot, per-token advance, no re-parse of concatenated text.
- --det-draft-n-max: -1=all, 0=disabled, >0 caps filter output and is copied to --spec-draft-n-max (auto-derive only when > 0).
- --det-draft-accept-all: skip target verification, filter is verifier
- Auto-derive --spec-draft-n-max from --det-draft-n-max (only when > 0)
- Benchmark tool with --compare, --n-runs, --det-draft-accept-all, --det-draft-language support.

The goal here is to provide a control mechanism for domain specific cases where speculation is not acceptable and the problem is well known.
This is a novel enhancement based on a time tested well known grammar based solution, instead of this being likely correct it is either correct or not. 

In addition since a grammar based intercept is cheaper and simpler than the heavy sampling of the target model it is also faster as benchmarks reveal. This is more evident in CPU only edge devices like the N100.
With the --det-draft-accept-all enabled the plugin is fully responsible for all verification, the target model is removed from the decision making.

In the default case, invalid tokens are pruned while the bonus token is verified by the target model. In the case where fewer tokens are accepted by the target model than what was verified by the plugin, the `deterministic_draft_rollback` rewinds the matcher to match what was emitted by the target model. The per-step final token is grammar-constrained before emission (post-fix; zero desync events observed since).
In short the real benefit is with the --det-draft-accept-all.
In this mode, the grammar is the sole verifier, the target model does no rejection sampling. Output distribution follows the grammar-constrained draft, not the target model an opt-in tradeoff.

Original RFC Link: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/25219

** sample results **
Grammar-verified speculative decoding with a pluggable SDK. Every emitted token passes the grammar in both modes. Zero `commit_token reject` lines across all runs.

### RTX 3060 (CUDA) - GPU

| Mode | Language | Model | n-max | MTP only | MTP + Filter | Speedup |
|------|----------|-------|-------|----------|--------------|---------|
| Accept-all | C | 2B | 16 | 1.10 t/s | 22.54 t/s | 20.5x |
| Accept-all | Java | 2B | 16 | 1.11 t/s | 15.62 t/s | 14.1x |
| Accept-all | JavaScript | 2B | 16 | 0.79 t/s | 22.90 t/s | 29.1x |
| Accept-all | Python | 2B | 16 | 2.11 t/s | 17.55 t/s | 8.3x |
| Default | C | 2B | 16 | 1.06 t/s | 2.01 t/s | 1.9x |
| Default | Java | 2B | 16 | 1.11 t/s | 1.23 t/s | 1.1x |
| Default | JavaScript | 2B | 16 | 0.98 t/s | 2.04 t/s | 2.1x |
| Default | Python | 2B | 16 | 2.08 t/s | 5.87 t/s | 2.8x |

### N100 (CPU-only oneAPI, 4C/4T Alder Lake-N)

| Mode | Language | Model | n-max | MTP only | MTP + Filter | Speedup |
|------|----------|-------|-------|----------|--------------|---------|
| Accept-all | C | 4B mxfp4 | 64 | 0.35 t/s | 5.97 t/s | 17.0x |
| Default | C | 4B mxfp4 | 16 | 2.02 t/s | 2.68 t/s | 1.3x |
| Default | C | 2B Q6_K | 16 | 4.38 t/s | 5.54 t/s | 1.3x |

N100 results report C only. The multi-language test was run before the n-max tuning with n-max 100 on a 4-core CPU, default-mode Java and JavaScript runs exceeded
the 1-hour timeout and Python managed 0.88 t/s, because low acceptance means nearly all
of the oversized draft is wasted compute (see the Tuning Cautionary Note in
benchmark-overview.md). That failure is what the n-max 16/64 guidance comes from.

### Key Observations

- **Accept-all** skips target model verification; grammar is sole verifier. Speedups measure a different algorithm than default mode.
- **Default mode** target-verifies all filter-accepted tokens. Speedup is real but modest.
- **n-max matters**: on weak CPUs, oversized n-max (100) wastes draft compute (0.21x). Properly tuned (16-64) gives 1.3-17x.
- **Low baseline MTP acceptance** (3.8%-17.6% on N100 fine-tunes): speculative decoding alone is nearly worthless; the filter makes it viable.
- **Output validity**: 0/1 in all N100 runs (models write broken C). Filter guarantees grammar-valid tokens, not gcc-clean programs -- CFGs cannot check static semantics.

All numbers: single-run, n_runs=1, indicative not statistical. See benchmark-overview.md for full methodology.

title: server : allow RANK pooling batch splitting for causal LLM rerankers (ie. Qwen3 and Qwen3-VL)
body:
## Overview
Traditionally, rerank models were bidirectional cross-encoders like BERT, which mandated that all the tokens in the input must be within the same physical batch due to bidirectional attention. However, the Qwen3 and Qwen3-VL family of rerankers are just repurposed LLMs (causal decoders). This meant that prefill does not have to be all within the same physical batch. They can be chunked into batches just like any other decoder LLM. 

Currently, llama-server is outdated in enforcing this difference. llama-server is too conservative and forces all rerank models to have to batch their prefill into one physical batch (default 512 tokens). _**In other words, if the document is greater than the physical batch size, the rerank doesn't work**_. Thus, long documents or images cannot be fed into the rerank model in llama.cpp

## Code Changes
~~Expose llama_model_rank_pooling_is_causal (and the internal llm_arch_rank_pooling_is_causal) so the server can tell whether a RANK-pooling model reads the last token (causal LLM reranker, e.g. Qwen3) or needs the whole sequence at once (bidirectional encoder, e.g. BERT).~~

1. Expose llama_get_causal_attn(ctx) so the server can check the effective runtime attention type, reflecting any --attention override or set_causal_attn call. (cparams).
2. Also expose llama_model_is_causal() so the server can make a generic causal/non-causal decision based off the model gguf metadata (hparams).
~~2. Set hparams.causal_attn = false on all bidirectional BERT variants (bert, eurobert, jina-bert-v2/v3, modern-bert, neo-bert, nomic-bert, nomic-bert-moe) where it was previously an oversight.~~
3. can_split() now permits chunked prefill for causal RANK models instead of rejecting inputs larger than n_ubatch. The graph builder's inline arch check is refactored to use the same cparams.causal_attn predicate, removing the duplication.

## Additional information

This first PR is in support of adding full multimodal support for the /embedding and /rerank endpoints. See here for more context (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/18665#issuecomment-5544533094)

title: llama + CUDA: flash_attn_ext_rows (fix unified kv for multi-seq)
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

During multi-seq inference, unified kv-cache pays a big penalty due to having to filter out other sequence tokens from the mask. This PR introduces an extension to flash attention (`flash_attn_ext_rows`) which when supported by a backend allows llama.cpp to send an optimized representation of the query. Queries shared the kv rows and their mask + a new data struct `kv_rows` enables an indirect look-up for a compact representation of the required tokens per seq.

title: bug: fix grammar builder crash on invalid minItems/maxItems (#29462)
body:
Closes #29462

### Description
A JSON schema request specifying an array with `minItems` greater than `maxItems` (e.g. `minItems: 10, maxItems: 2`) or a direct GBNF pattern like `root ::= "a"{10,2}` caused a fatal Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash in `llama-server`. 

The crash happened because `llama-grammar.cpp` performed unsigned arithmetic (`max_times - min_times`) without verifying that `min_times <= max_times`. When `min > max`, this subtraction underflowed, resulting in a gigantic `n_opt` count (~18 quintillion), driving the server to immediately exhaust all available memory and crash with `std::bad_alloc`.

This PR:
1. Adds a guard in `json-schema-to-grammar.cpp` (`build_repetition`) to gracefully clamp `max_items = min_items` when contradictory bounds are provided in the schema.
2. Adds a strict safety check in `llama-grammar.cpp`'s `handle_repetitions` to throw a clean `std::runtime_error` if `min_times > max_times` ever reaches the engine, preventing the unbounded allocation loop.

title: ggml-rpc : fix out-of-bounds write in SET_ROWS graph execution
body:
## Overview

This PR fixes out-of-bounds (OOB) vulnerabilities in the RPC server caused by malformed `GGML_OP_SET_ROWS` and `GGML_OP_GET_ROWS` tensors. It introduces a pre-execution validation loop in `rpc_server::graph_compute` to verify specific tensor dimensions before handing the graph over to the backend:

- For `GGML_OP_SET_ROWS`, it verifies that the `ne[2]` and `ne[3]` dimensions of the `node` and `src[0]` strictly match.
- For `GGML_OP_GET_ROWS`, it verifies that the `ne[2]` dimension of `src[0]` strictly matches the `ne[1]` dimension of `src[1]`.

If a mismatch is detected, the server logs an error and safely aborts the request, preventing memory corruption and out-of-bounds memory exposure.

## Additional information

Fixes #26912 and fixes #26825.

Previously, a malformed network packet could bypass the local `ggml_set_rows` and `ggml_get_rows` assertions. This caused `ggml_backend_graph_compute` to either write past the allocated buffer bounds (`SET_ROWS`) or read past the `src0` buffer and copy unowned memory into the output tensor (`GET_ROWS`), which could then be retrieved via `GET_TENSOR`. This patch safely catches these shape mismatches at the network boundary.

title: tools/quantize: add --verify for per-tensor quantization error
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

Adds `--verify` (and `--verify-max-error`) to `llama-quantize`.

After a normal quantize run, it reloads the input and output GGUF, dequantizes each tensor, and prints one JSON object with per-tensor `max_abs_error`, `rms_error`, and a 150-bucket `|diff|` histogram. Non-finite values come out as `null` so the JSON still parses.

Exit codes:
- `0` — ok
- `1` — structural problem (missing tensor, bad read, etc.)
- `2` — some tensor's `max_abs_error` is over `--verify-max-error` (default `1.0`)

JSON always prints before a gate exit, so you keep the numbers either way. Off by default — no behavior change unless you pass `--verify`. Refuses `--dry-run` and `--keep-split`.

Why: today you mostly eyeball perplexity or run `test-quantize-stats` by hand. This puts a machine-readable check on the tool people already run, so a script can catch a truncated file or bad scales.

Checked on Tiny-LLM F16 → Q8_0 against `test-quantize-stats -p` (same digits). Corrupt 1 KB of the output → `max_abs_error` spikes, exit `2`, names the tensor. Truncate the output → exit `1`.

## Additional information

Default gate of `1.0` is deliberate: healthy Q8_0 / Q4_K_M errors I measured were ~0.001–0.03; a 1 KB corruption was ~7e5. Raise it with `--verify-max-error` if your weights are large enough that real quant error can exceed 1.0. Histogram constants match `test-quantize-stats`.

title: server: don't store the draft KV in context checkpoints
body:
## Overview

Context checkpoints are written with `LLAMA_STATE_SEQ_FLAGS_PARTIAL_ONLY`, which asks for only the parts of the memory that cannot be rolled back.

`llama_memory_hybrid::state_write()` implements that by skipping `mem_attn` and writing only `mem_recr`, and `state_read()` does the same on the way back, so the target's attention cache is deliberately left out of every checkpoint and stays resident:

```cpp
// src/llama-memory-hybrid.cpp
if ((flags & LLAMA_STATE_SEQ_FLAGS_PARTIAL_ONLY) == 0) {
    mem_attn->state_write(io, seq_id, flags);
}
mem_recr->state_write(io, seq_id, flags);
```

The draft model's context is a plain `llama_kv_cache` — a prefix-addressed attention cache, the same kind of memory as `mem_attn`. But `llama_kv_cache::state_write()` discards the flags and serializes every cell, so the `PARTIAL_ONLY` request has no effect on it:

```cpp
// src/llama-kv-cache.cpp:2180
void llama_kv_cache::state_write(llama_io_wstr_i & io, llama_seq_id seq_id, llama_state_seq_flags flags) const {
    GGML_UNUSED(flags);
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < cells.size(); ++i) {
```

So the whole draft KV ends up in every checkpoint. Since the draft is sized to the target's `n_ctx`, checkpoint size grows linearly with the context instead of being the constant cost of the recurrent state.

Skip the draft when creating a long-term checkpoint.

## Measured

Qwen3.8-27B (16 attention + 48 recurrent layers), MTP draft, q8_0 KV, `-c 262144`, `-ctxcp 144`, checkpoints 1..8 over a 13789-token prompt:

| checkpoint (n_tokens) | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (2048) | 157.673 MiB | **149.626 MiB** |
| 2 (4097) | 165.724 MiB | **149.626 MiB** |
| 3 (6146) | 173.775 MiB | **149.626 MiB** |
| 4 (8195) | 181.825 MiB | **149.626 MiB** |
| 5 (10244) | 189.876 MiB | **149.626 MiB** |
| 6 (12293) | 197.927 MiB | **149.626 MiB** |
| 7 (13273) | 201.778 MiB | **149.626 MiB** |
| 8 (13771) | 203.734 MiB | **149.626 MiB** |

The slope is 46.061 MiB over 11723 tokens, i.e. **4.02 KiB per token**, and extrapolating it to zero tokens lands exactly on the 149.626 MiB that the recurrent state alone costs (which is `RS buffer / (1 + n_rs_seq)`, as expected).

The draft term therefore overtakes the recurrent state around 38k tokens, and at 256k it is 1.0 GiB per checkpoint — over the 144 checkpoints `-ctxcp` allows that is ~150 GiB instead of ~21 GiB.

Greedy output and draft acceptance are unchanged.

## Why no matching change on the way back

The draft's cells are position-addressed and survive like `mem_attn`'s, and the restore path already tolerates a checkpoint without draft data:

- `common_prompt_checkpoint::load_dft()` returns early when `data_dft.empty()` (`common/common.cpp`), so the draft memory is left untouched rather than cleared.
- The `clear()` in `llama_kv_cache::state_read_sinfo()` is guarded by `seq_id == -1`, and an empty per-stream cell count is skipped outright, so loading a partial state does not wipe the cache.

The per-draft-step rollback checkpoint in `slot.spec_ckpt` is untouched: it goes through `update_dft()` directly with `ON_DEVICE` and does not depend on the long-term checkpoints.

title: [Security]: prevent out-of-bounds accesses from malformed mmproj files
body:
The allocation used the declared slot sizes while the copy used the tensors from the graph. Use the graph tensors for both so the size cannot disagree.

## Security context

**`state_out` heap out-of-bounds write (gen-audio / pocket-tts path).** The graph of a gen-audio mmproj exposes `state_out_<slot>` tensors whose shapes are fully determined by the projector's weights and metadata. `list_gen_state_slots()` reports the *declared* slot sizes, and the `state_out` buffer was sized from those, while the copy loop pulls `ggml_nbytes(t)` bytes out of the *graph* tensors. Nothing makes the two agree: a crafted mmproj can declare small state slots while making the graph's state tensors larger, and each encode then writes past the end of `state_out` - a heap out-of-bounds write whose length and contents are chosen by the projector file, repeated on every generation flush. Depending on the layout this is silent corruption or a crash (heap-buffer-overflow under ASan).

The only attacker-controlled input is the mmproj passed to `--mmproj`; the text model and the CLI invocation are the victim's own.

With this change the graph tensors are resolved first and `state_out` is sized from `ggml_nbytes()` of exactly those tensors, then exactly that many bytes are copied per tensor, so the allocation and the copy cannot disagree by construction.

**`feature_layer` hardening.** Master already rejects indices above `n_layer` (#29276); this additionally rejects negative indices (conversions are expected to standardize on non-negative values) and includes the key name and the valid range in the error message.

## Testing

- crafted mmproj declaring small state slots with oversized graph state tensors: before, ASan reports a heap-buffer-overflow in the `state_out` copy path; after, the encode completes with `state_out` sized to the graph tensors
- well-formed gen-audio projectors: the graph tensors match the declared slots, so `state_out` layout is unchanged and generation is unaffected

title: cuda: FWHT kernels for block widths above 512
body:
## Overview

The CUDA FWHT covers block widths 64 to 512. It runs one row per warp and keeps `N/32`
values per lane, so wider blocks need more registers per lane than that layout allows.

`fwht_cuda_block` runs one row per thread block with 256 threads, so each thread keeps
`N/256` values instead. Stages below the warp width still shuffle, those up to the block
width go through shared memory, and the rest stay in registers. The butterfly and sign
convention match the existing kernel.

Widths 64 to 512 keep the warp kernel and are untouched. 1024 through 8192 use the new
one, for both F32 and F16 sources.

This is the CUDA counterpart to #29095 (Metal). Stacked on #29096; the last commit is the
one to review here.

## Additional information

Tested on an H100 PCIe (compute capability 9.0, CUDA 12.8, `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=90`):

- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT_HADAMARD` 25/25, including the new 1024/2048/4096/8192 cases
  in F32 and F16, and the 16384 case that falls back
- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT` 1297/1297, no regressions

A passing suite does not by itself show the new kernel ran, since a Hadamard-hinted matmul that
falls back to the generic path computes the same values. To confirm the wide kernel is actually
selected I temporarily made `fwht_cuda_block` scale its output by 2 and re-ran, which gave
15/25 with exactly ten failures:

- the ten wide cases, 1024/2048/4096/8192 and 1024 with seven rows, in both F32 and F16, all failed
- all fourteen cases at 512 and below passed, which is the warp kernel that change does not touch
- 16384 also passed, confirming widths outside the supported list still take the generic path

The change was reverted and the binary rebuilt before the numbers above were taken.

8192 allocates 32 KB of shared memory per block, within the 48 KB default limit. If that is too
aggressive for older parts I am happy to cap the width list lower.

title: server: sanitize invalid UTF-8 in generated text at the token boundary
body:
## Overview

Byte-level BPE vocabularies contain pieces that decode to invalid UTF-8 (e.g. lone continuation bytes), and models occasionally sample them mid-generation. On llama-server the final parse then fails with "The model produced output that does not match the expected peg-native format" (or the Content-only equivalent on /completions), and an HTTP 500 occurs, and no text after the bad byte is ever streamed.

Reproduced on unpatched master with Ling 3.0 tiny at Q8_K_XL and at BF16 (the release dtype): emoji-heavy checklist generations produced invalid emissions at roughly 1 per 11k and 1 per 39k tokens respectively, byte signature e2 9c 85 followed by a lone 0x85 piece after a valid U+2705. 

This sanitizes generated text at the accumulation and finalization boundaries in server-common: invalid sequences are replaced with U+FFFD; trailing incomplete sequences are held back while streaming and dropped at finalization. Strict parsing is unchanged. The replacement diverges from the token stream by the replaced bytes; the current behavior loses the entire turn to a 500.

## Additional information

vLLM handles the same class at the detokenizer boundary (vllm-project/vllm#17448).  SGLang's incremental detokenizer handles the same class at the boundary as well: text ending in U+FFFD is held back and retried with subsequent tokens (`detokenizer_manager.py`).  

The invalid pieces were discovered on Ling 3.0 Flash, but are not Ling-specific. The Qwen3 and DeepSeek-V4 vocabularies also contain them (944 and 1,470 invalid-UTF-8 pieces respectively, including a lone 0x85).

Verified no output change on a non-Ling model (Qwen3.5-9B): greedy completions under this patch are byte-identical to unpatched master.

Ling 3.0 Flash requires this, together with #28682.

## Overview

Ling 3.0 templates pre-open <think> in the generation prompt, so the model never emits an opening tag and tool calls can appear before `</think>`. The generated parser classified that output entirely as `reasoning_content` and clients received `content=""` with no `tool_calls`.

Adds the Ling 3.0 Flash chat template (byte-identical to the GGUF-embedded template) and tests covering the unclosed-think tool call (full and streaming), closed-think paths, trailing prose, parallel calls, marker-like strings in argument values, and `reasoning_format=none`.

title: webui: exclude server liveness endpoints from service worker cache (#28444)
body:
**Overview**

Reproduced on a build of master with the PWA service worker installed:

1. Start llama-server, open the web UI, let it load once.
2. Stop the server.
3. Reload the page.

The UI still renders as connected, and it stays that way across a browser restart and a manual cache clear — which matches what the reporter describes in #28444.

The cause is in the service worker's runtime caching. /health and /props are matched by API_CACHING_PATTERNS.STATIC_API and handled with NetworkFirst, cached in api-cache for API_CACHE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS (24h). NetworkFirst falls back to the cache when the request fails, so once those two responses have been cached, a stopped server no longer produces a failed liveness check: the service worker answers from cache and the UI concludes the server is up. Clearing the browser cache does not help because the entry lives in the service worker's own Cache Storage.

The patch removes health and props from that pattern, so server availability is always resolved from a live request. /models, /tools, /slots, /cors-proxy and /v1 keep the caching they had.

One consequence worth your call: offline PWA use will now show the server as down rather than showing a stale but populated UI. That looks right for a liveness check, but if you would rather keep /props cached and exclude only /health, it is a one-word change.

**Additional information**

Fixes #28444.

The added unit test asserts that /health and /props match none of the caching patterns while the four data endpoints still do. It fails if the constant is reverted.

body:
I hit this running Claude Code against a local llama.cpp server. Compaction failed with "summarization produced empty response" and the only workaround was /clear.

title: metal : wide query tile for kernel_flash_attn_ext
body:
## Overview

The current flash-attention kernel processes 8 query rows for each K/V tile it loads. The main idea in this PR is to reuse that same K/V data for 16 query rows instead, so each K/V load does twice as much query work.

`kernel_flash_attn_ext` already takes the number of queries per threadgroup `Q` as a template parameter, but the QK^T and P*V simdgroup-matrix blocks only process the first 8 query rows, and only `Q = 8` is instantiated. This PR makes those blocks iterate over all `Q/8` query blocks and adds `Q = 16` with `nsg = 4` and `nsg = 8`.

Whether the 16-row tile is faster depends on the device and shape, so it is selected through the tuning table, like `fa_vec_pick`. Only `GGML_METAL_DEVICE_M5` has rows in this PR, and M5 is not a family representative, so other devices keep the existing dispatch.

The first version of this PR used a shape-only gate and always ran the 16-row tile with `nsg = 8`. That regressed on M4 Max (see @forforever73's table below), so the gate was replaced by the tuning table as suggested.

---

### Dispatch

`ggml_metal_tuning::fa_pick` maps `(device, DK, DV, ne11 bucket)` to `(Q, NSG)`. It first looks for an exact `ne11` bucket, then a `FA_NE11_DEFAULT` row, first for the device and then for its family representative.

If nothing matches, the existing dispatch is used. M5 is not the representative of any family, so its 25 rows are not used by another device.

The 8-row tile is always used when:

* `ne01 < 64`
* `ne01 < 256` and the last wide tile would hold only 1..8 rows. It would pad 8 more rows than the 8-row tile, which costs 2–4% at KV 4096 on M5 (`ne01 = 68`: 0.96x).
* K/V are not F16 and are not dequantized to F16 up front through `use_kv_f16`. BF16/F32 K/V and the in-kernel dequantization branches are unchanged.
* `GGML_PAD(DV, 64) % (16*NSG) != 0`
* The threadgroup memory would exceed the device limit (320/256 and 576/512 at 32 KiB).

The wide tile is only instantiated for the F16 kernels, which keeps library load time close to master. A cold compile of the `fa` library with an empty shader cache goes from 13.6 s to 14.2 s on M5. The `blk` buffer stays sized for the 8-row tile, which is an upper bound for the 16-row one.

---

### Tuning

`ggml-metal-tuning fa` generates the table rows. The sweep took about 20 minutes on M5.

The tuner compares the 8-row tile against `Q = 16` with `nsg = 4` and `nsg = 8`, using F16 K/V and GQA 8. GQA 8 had the smallest gains in the measurements below. The sweep covers 13 head sizes, 8 KV lengths from 512 to 65536, and up to 4 batch sizes, including a partial last tile.

A bucket gets a row only if the candidate is no slower than the 8-row tile at every sampled point and at least 2% faster overall. `nsg = 8` is selected over `nsg = 4` only when it is at least 3% faster. On M5, hs 96, 192, and 256 lose at some point with KV < 4096 and get no row there.

`nsg` is part of the table because no single value works for every head size. `Q = 8` with `nsg = 8` is slower than master's `Q = 8, nsg = 4` in every case measured on M5 (0.77–0.99x).

For `Q = 16`, geometric mean speedup vs master over the tuner's 30 sample points per head size is:

| Head | `Q = 16, nsg = 4` | `Q = 16, nsg = 8` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 64/64 | 1.166 (0) | 1.007 (2) |
| 128/128 | 1.166 (0) | 1.147 (0) |
| 256/256 | 1.035 (13) | 1.099 (3) |

> *The number in parentheses denotes the count of sampled points slower than master.*

With `nsg = 4`, hs 256 loses at almost every point with KV $\le$ 4096 (0.89–1.00x). With `nsg = 8`, hs 64 gains almost nothing. The three hs 256 points where `nsg = 8` loses are at KV < 4096, where hs 256 gets no row. Master's `nsg = ne00 >= 512 ? 8 : 4` still applies to the 8-row tile.

Whether `Q = 16` helps on M4 Max requires running the tuner on that hardware. A device only uses the wide tile once it has rows in `fa_tuned_table`, and a run that emits nothing indicates it should stay on the 8-row tile. Rows for other devices can be added once profiled.

---

### Adding a Device

To generate rows for another Metal device:

1. **Build the tuner and test targets:**
```sh
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j --target ggml-metal-tuning test-backend-ops llama-bench

```


2. **Run the tuner:**
```sh
./build/bin/ggml-metal-tuning fa > fa_rows.txt 2> fa_sweep.log

```


* Takes ~20 minutes on M5.
* `fa_rows.txt` contains rows ready to add to `fa_tuned_table`. An empty file indicates the wide tile did not outperform the baseline.
* `fa_sweep.log` contains detailed per-point measurements.


3. **Verify correctness and benchmark:**
```sh
# Correctness check
./build/bin/test-backend-ops test -b MTL0 -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT

# Microbenchmarks
./build/bin/test-backend-ops perf -b MTL0 -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT -p 'nb=4096,'

# End-to-end performance
./build/bin/llama-bench -m <model> -fa 1 -ub 2048 -p 2048 \
  -d 0,2048,4096,8192,16384,32768 -r 1 -n 32 -t 1

```



> **Note:** The tuner prints the device token near the start of `fa_sweep.log`. If the device reports `GGML_METAL_DEVICE_GENERIC`, it must be explicitly defined in `ggml_metal_device_id` first to prevent generic rows from matching unspecified hardware.

---

### Performance

**Hardware:** Apple M5 (10-core GPU, 24 GB)

**Baseline:** Master `ec9281505`

*All results use the `(Q, NSG)` selected by the M5 tuning rows.*

```sh
./build/bin/test-backend-ops perf -b MTL0 -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT -p 'nb=4096,'

```

Speedup in % (positive = PR is faster). Values represent the median of three paired runs per case:

| hs / GQA | kv = 4096 | kv = 8192 | kv = 16384 | kv = 32768 | kv = 65536 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **hs64 / g1** | +16.0% | +33.1% | +53.5% | +66.2% | +72.2% |
| **hs64 / g4** | +13.3% | +16.2% | +25.1% | +41.8% | +52.9% |
| **hs64 / g8** | +12.7% | +15.3% | +22.0% | +35.0% | +47.8% |
| **hs128 / g1** | +20.1% | +35.3% | +41.4% | +46.7% | +36.2% |
| **hs128 / g4** | +9.9% | +23.7% | +33.0% | +35.8% | +29.8% |
| **hs128 / g8** | +10.8% | +19.9% | +32.5% | +34.6% | +30.8% |
| **hs256 / g1** | +18.4% | +28.0% | +41.5% | +59.5% | +66.0% |
| **hs256 / g4** | +18.9% | +19.0% | +23.6% | +19.1% | +26.3% |
| **hs256 / g8** | +18.8% | +18.9% | +22.0% | +16.3% | +22.2% |

* The speedup is largest without GQA, remaining positive across all head sizes and context lengths on M5.
* At hs 256 and KV 65536, the 16-row tile executes in 54–57 ms per query head regardless of GQA. The 8-row tile requires 62–67 ms with shared K/V heads and ~100 ms when unshared.
* For shapes remaining on the 8-row tile, `DK/DV = 576/512` shows a delta of +0.2% to +4.6% (mostly under +2%). Forcing `gpt-oss-20b` onto the 8-row tile yields 0.99–1.00x end-to-end at all context depths.

---

### End-to-End Benchmarks

```sh
./build/bin/llama-bench -m <model> -fa 1 -ub 2048 -p 2048 -d 0,2048,4096,8192,16384,32768 -r 1 -n 32 -t 1

```

*Values represent the mean of two alternating runs between master and PR. The `d65536` rows were evaluated separately.*

#### Tiel-Coder-35B-A3B IQ3_XXS

*(hs 256, GQA 8, full attention in 1 of 4 layers)*

| Test | Master (t/s) | PR (t/s) | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pp2048` | 732.93 | 739.45 | **1.009x** |
| `pp2048@d2048` | 661.59 | 671.37 | **1.015x** |
| `pp2048@d4096` | 600.04 | 624.41 | **1.041x** |
| `pp2048@d8192` | 508.65 | 536.88 | **1.055x** |
| `pp2048@d16384` | 393.45 | 426.27 | **1.083x** |
| `pp2048@d32768` | 261.73 | 284.72 | **1.088x** |
| `pp2048@d65536` | 155.11 | 173.97 | **1.122x** |

#### Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M

*(hs 256, GQA 4, full attention in 1 of 4 layers)*

| Test | Master (t/s) | PR (t/s) | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pp2048` | 358.91 | 371.39 | **1.035x** |
| `pp2048@d2048` | 349.64 | 352.77 | **1.009x** |
| `pp2048@d4096` | 337.12 | 335.91 | **0.996x** |
| `pp2048@d8192` | 309.03 | 320.37 | **1.037x** |
| `pp2048@d16384` | 270.38 | 288.60 | **1.067x** |
| `pp2048@d32768` | 208.67 | 228.21 | **1.094x** |

#### gpt-oss-20b MXFP4

*(hs 64, GQA 8, sinks, SWA in every other layer)*

| Test | Master (t/s) | PR (t/s) | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pp2048` | 825.79 | 836.03 | **1.012x** |
| `pp2048@d2048` | 719.37 | 737.35 | **1.025x** |
| `pp2048@d4096` | 637.08 | 661.16 | **1.038x** |
| `pp2048@d8192` | 520.71 | 548.07 | **1.053x** |
| `pp2048@d16384` | 375.40 | 411.92 | **1.097x** |
| `pp2048@d32768` | 220.91 | 269.29 | **1.219x** |
| `pp2048@d65536` | 111.92 | 145.20 | **1.297x** |

* Prefill gains scale with context depth. `gpt-oss-20b` shows the largest improvement because hs 64 achieves significant speedups under GQA 8 for KV $\ge$ 32768, and 50% of its layers run standard full attention.
* Run-to-run noise is roughly 2–3% on hs 256 models. The depth-0 configurations use the baseline 8-row tile, aligning with the 1.009x and 1.035x measurements. The 0.996x Qwen3.5 result at d4096 falls within normal variance.
* `tg32` generation throughput fluctuated marginally between 0.98x and 1.05x across all three models. Token generation (decoding) does not invoke this kernel.

---

### Testing

#### Operator Suite

```sh
./build/bin/test-backend-ops test -b MTL0 -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT

```

* **Status:** Passed 4951/4951 tests.
* Includes the standard `fa_vec` slice (240/240) and an added wide tile test slice (720/720).
* The added test slice forces `Q = 16` via an internal override mechanism so systems lacking device-specific rows still exercise the wide-tile codepath. It validates 15 head sizes across `nsg = 4/8`, attention sinks, GQA 4, full and partial tiles, kvpad, and three storage types:
* **F16:** Dispatches wide tile.
* **Q8_0:** Upfront dequantization to F16, followed by wide tile.
* **BF16 / Large Dimensions (320/256, 576/512):** Retained on the 8-row tile.

title: ggml-cpu : add Q8_0 IME1 matrix kernel for SpacemiT X60
body:
## Overview

I have a Milk-V Jupiter board and wanted Q8_0 to run properly on the SpacemiT X60. The X60 already
had IME acceleration, but only for Q4_0/Q4_1/Q4_K. Q8_0 had no IME1 kernel at all, and because the
SpacemiT build sets `GGML_CPU_REPACK=OFF`, there was no repack path compiled in either — so Q8_0
had no accelerated path whatsoever and ran at about a tenth of Q4_0's prefill speed on the same
board. This PR adds the missing Q8_0 IME1 kernel.

This replaces #28025, which I closed. That version was M1-only and reached 39.97 t/s prefill;
this one adds the 4-row path, which roughly doubles it again.

## Additional information

Changes:

- `make_block_q8_0x16` and the repack entry in `repack.cpp`: interleave Q8_0 weights into the
  16-column layout the IME1 `vmadot` sequence expects.
- `ime1::gemm_kernel_i8i8` in `ime1_kernels.cpp`: the int8 x int8 IME1 kernel, with both a single-row
  and a 4-row A path. The 4-row path loads each B panel once and reuses it across 4 rows of A, which
  is where most of the gain over the M1-only version comes from.
- `quantize_a_4row_i8`: the 4-row activation quantization the M4 path needs. In #28025 this was
  `nullptr` and `gemm_m >= 4` was forced back through the single-row path.
- wiring in `forward_mul_mat` and the repack factory for `block_q8_0`.
- docs: mark Q8_0 as supported on X60.

## Testing

Milk-V Jupiter (SpacemiT X60, 8 cores / 4 preferred, RVV1.0, VLEN=256), Bianbu 2.1.1, gcc 14.2.
Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, `llama-bench`, `-t 4` under `taskset -c 0-3`, 5 repetitions, board otherwise
idle.

Correctness: I compared the kernel against a quant-exact reference (dequantizing the same blocks and
doing the multiply in integer arithmetic, rather than against a float reference) for K = 32 up to
4096. Max relative error is ~1e-6, which is the expected float accumulation difference. I also
checked that generation stays coherent across several prompts.

Note that `test-backend-ops` does not exercise this kernel on a CPU-only build: it skips the CPU
backend and reports OK, so it cannot be used to validate this change.

Performance, pp128 prefill, before and after this change on the same build settings (both with IME1
enabled, so the only variable is the kernel):

| model             | before    | after     | speedup |
| ----------------- | --------: | --------: | ------: |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B Q8_0 | 10.70 t/s | 95.27 t/s |    8.9x |

The commit message quotes another run (Q8_0 93.87 t/s, Q4_0 107.51 t/s); the difference is
run-to-run variation.

For reference, Q4_0 on the same board measures 107.81 t/s with this change applied, against 106.40 t/s
before it, i.e. unchanged within run-to-run variation, which is what I would expect since this PR
does not touch that path.

I am only claiming prefill here. Token generation does improve, but Q4_0 token generation moved by
about 1.19x between the two builds despite that path being untouched, so I do not trust the
token-generation numbers enough to quote them as a result of this change.

title: llama : fix K/V and recurrent state cleanup after failed restores
body:
## Overview

A failed per-sequence state restore can remove sequence metadata while leaving K/V or recurrent-state tensor data written by the failed restore.

Buffer-backed restores can also leave deferred writes pending, allowing them to be applied after cleanup.

This PR contains failed restores by:

* clearing affected K/V or recurrent-state tensor data;
* discarding deferred writes after cleanup and before the reader is destroyed;
* applying the same deferred-write cleanup to whole-context buffer restores;
* validating restored `cell_count` values before they are used for allocation or target-range setup;
* cleaning up an already-restored attention state when a later recurrent-memory restore fails in `llama_memory_hybrid`.

Failures before modifying the target sequence leave it unchanged. After modification, the affected state is removed rather than attempting transactional rollback. For `llama_memory_hybrid`, if the attention component has already been restored and the recurrent component then fails, the restored attention state is also cleared.

Fixes #27068.

## Additional information

The original issue was observed in the K/V cache, but the same failure-cleanup behavior is needed for recurrent memory.

Tensor cleanup is only performed after a valid target range has been established, so failures during metadata parsing do not clear unrelated cells.

Per-sequence restore now also validates `cell_count` against the available cache or recurrent-memory capacity before using it.

For `llama_memory_hybrid`, restore is sequential across the attention and recurrent components. If the recurrent restore throws after the attention restore has succeeded, the attention state restored for that sequence is cleared before the exception is rethrown.

The cleanup runs only on restore failure and does not affect successful restore or normal decoding.

### Tests

Added failed-restore regression coverage to `test-save-load-state`. Test 9 exercises corrupted buffer and file restores and runs through the existing architecture coverage, including hybrid models.

The test verifies that a failed restore leaves the affected sequence empty and does not leave tensor data that changes the logits of another sequence.

Local validation:

* `ctest`: 62/62 passed.
* Sequential run across 127 generated models: Test 9 PASS 123 / SKIP 4 / FAIL 0. The four skipped models (`dream`, `llada`, `llada-moe`, and `rnd1`) do not have memory.

CUDA validation and server-level fault injection with K/V and hybrid recurrent memory were also performed on an earlier base.

### Non-goal

This does not provide transactional restore. If a failed restore has already modified the target sequence, its previous contents are not reconstructed.

Cross-component cleanup is handled for `llama_memory_hybrid`, where attention restore can precede a failing recurrent restore. Equivalent cleanup for the other composite memory implementations (`llama_kv_cache_iswa`, `llama_memory_hybrid_iswa`, `llama_kv_cache_dsa_iswa`, and `llama_kv_cache_msa`) is not addressed by this PR.

The separate ON_DEVICE pre-validation issue is tracked in #27439.

title: server: roll back batch state after slot exceptions
body:
## Overview

Fixes a `llama-server` exception-safety issue where a failed slot could leave partial state in the shared batch and later trigger a process-level abort.

During `pre_decode()`, a slot may append tokens or embeddings and update related state before a later operation throws. Previously, `iterate()` released the failed slot without rolling back those partial changes, which could leave inconsistent state such as:

```cpp
batch.size() > 0 && batch.slot_batched == nullptr
```

and later trigger:

```cpp
GGML_ASSERT(batch.slot_batched || batch.size() == 0);
```

This PR adds per-slot rollback for unrendered batch state. On exception, it restores the previous batch sizes and metadata, resets temporary speculative / aLoRA state, clears the failed slot's prompt state, and preserves work already added by healthy slots.

It also moves `batch.clear()` to the start of `pre_decode()` so the batch-building phase is consistently rollback-safe, and skips slot pointers that have already been released.

## Additional information

Related issue: #29391

This does not fix the underlying cause of the reported `std::bad_alloc`. It prevents a slot-local exception from corrupting shared batch state and escalating into a server-wide failure.

Regression tests use deterministic fault injection to throw `std::bad_alloc` after a slot has already modified the batch.

The tests cover:

- prompt and generation phases;
- single-slot and multi-slot continuous batching;
- failures in different slot positions;
- preservation of healthy requests and their generated tokens;
- server health after the failed request;
- cleanup of the failed slot's prompt/cache state;
- successful retry after rollback;
- normal prompt-cache reuse after recovery.

The rollback only stores vector sizes and a small amount of metadata; it does not copy the full batch.

title: kv-cache : fix iSWA seq_pos_max answering from the SWA cache only
body:
## Overview

`llama_kv_cache_iswa::seq_pos_max` answered from the SWA cache alone. After a partial `seq_rm` below the sliding window (e.g. keeping only the last few tokens of a long prompt), the SWA cache becomes empty while the base cache still holds cells, so `seq_pos_max` returned `-1` for a sequence that is not empty. Callers that derive positions from it (`llama_batch_get_one` via `llama_batch_allocr`) then restart at position 0 and silently overwrite live base-cache cells - the KV corruption reported in #29045.

The base cache is a superset of the SWA cache, so the fix reports the maximum across both caches:

```cpp
return std::max(kv_base->seq_pos_max(seq_id), kv_swa->seq_pos_max(seq_id));
```

This restores the documented contract that `-1` means "the sequence is empty". `seq_pos_min` already reports the minimum across both caches and is unchanged.

## Additional information

Fixes #29045. The fix direction matches what @juliusbangert proposed in the issue thread; the repro was confirmed on current master by @mitoyosh.

Validation: CPU-only build (`-DLLAMA_CURL=OFF`); `test-batch-alloc` (the `llama_batch_allocr` consumer of `seq_pos_max`) passes - 50 tests, 327 assertions, 0 failures. The repo has no dedicated iSWA unit-test harness, so no new regression test is included; the issue body has the minimal runtime repro. title: model: GraniteSpeech5ForCTC (Turbo CTC)
body:
## Overview

This PR adds support for the `GraniteSpeech5ForCTC` model architecture to support https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc. The model is non-autoregressive (encoder-only) and therefore introduces some net-new code paths discussed below.

## Additional information

`llama.cpp` has had support for `/v1/audio/transcriptions` for a while, but the implementation has only served to send audio to a full multimodal audio-llm with a prompt requesting transcription. This PR extends that entrypoint to support STT-only models like `granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc`, along with implementing support for that model architecture.

Along with this additional path through `tools/server` and `tools/common`, this model poses a challenge in both `tools/mtmd` and `libllama` itself: The core model is itself just an audio projector (nearly equivalent to the encoder in the `mmproj` for `granite-speech-4.x`), but rather than projecting this into text-token space and running it through an LLM backbone, the encoded audio is simply sent through an output layer and converted directly into `logits`. This makes the model extremely fast, but breaks a lot of assumptions in both `mtmd` and `libllama`.

To work through these issues, this PR introduces the following changes:

- Since all model-outputs are expected to derive from `libllama`, we couldn't directly pull from an `mtmd` model and skip `libllama` entirely for these models. This meant needing to split the logic between `mtmd` in a degenerate `mmproj` and `libllama` for the main encoder-only CTC-encoder model.
- New public method in `common.h`: `common_ctc_greedy_decode`. This implements the non-generative encode + greedy sampling needed by this model. It should generalize well to other models with similar encoder-only non-sampling styles, though the naming may be something we want to make more general to include future uses.
- New public method in `llama.h`: `llama_n_outputs`. This exposes the internal `n_outputs` from `llama_context` so that the greedy decoding can get the correct number of non-blank logits.
- Auto-expand `cparams.n_batch` / `cparams.n_ubatch` for non-decoder models in `llama_context`. These batching values are needed to support processing input sequences in batches for autoregressive models, but this model is single-shot, so needs to process the entire input in a single batch. This is _likely_ to be true of any such non-autoregressive model, but certainly up for discussion here.
- In `tools/server`, we need a fully new route for running `transcriptions` tasks using this kind of encoder-only model. We do this by checking whether the model needs logits, sampling, and memory, and if it is memory-free, requires logits, and doesn't require sampling, we use the new path that forwards through to `common_ctc_greedy_decode`, otherwise we use the old audio-LLM path.

## Open Questions

Given the number of new code-paths, there are a bunch of open questions here:

1. Does this kind of model even belong in `llama.cpp` instead of `whisper.cpp`? My main argument in favor of having the model here is one of distribution. `llama-server` (and https://llama.app) have become a user-facing distribution point and having these models supported here gives them reach both through the single server with `llama serve` and through downstream platforms that use `llama-server` directly (Ollama, LM Studio, AnythingLLM, etc).
2. Should we consider having this kind of model skip `libllama` _entirely_ and only live in `mtmd`? This would allow more code reuse between this architecture and `granite-speech`, but would require some more significant path changes in `common` and `server` to allow request handling to call pure-`mtmd` models.

title: ggml-cpu: Fix Flash Attention softcap handling for padded KV tiles on CPU
body:
## Overview

### Bug trigger conditions

This fixes a CPU Flash Attention issue when all of the following are true:

* `logit_softcap` is enabled;
* no attention mask is provided;
* the KV length is not a multiple of `GGML_FA_TILE_KV`.

The CPU implementation processes KV data in fixed-size tiles. For a partial KV tile, padded KQ entries must remain `-INFINITY` so that they receive zero weight in softmax.

### Root cause

Previously, KV padding was applied before softcap processing.

For padded entries, this effectively resulted in:

```text
-INFINITY -> tanh(-INFINITY) -> -logit_softcap
```

This converts the padding sentinel into a finite value inside the valid softcap logit range.

The padded entries can then contribute to the softmax normalization term, even though the corresponding padded V values do not contribute useful output values. This changes the attention result.

The issue is most visible just above the KV tile boundary. With `GGML_FA_TILE_KV = 64` and `KV = 65`, the second tile contains one valid KV entry and 63 padded entries.

When a mask is present, the issue can be hidden because the mask later restores the padded positions to `-INFINITY`.

### Fix

Apply softcap before writing the KV padding entries to `-INFINITY`.

The resulting order is:

```text
QK GEMM
scale
softcap
set padded KV logits to -INFINITY
mask
softmax
```

This guarantees that padded KV entries are still `-INFINITY` when they reach softmax.

The softcap computation for valid logits is unchanged. The fix does not add any buffers or additional processing passes, and keeps the existing full-tile vectorized `tanh` operation.

## Additional information

### Regression tests

Added unmasked Flash Attention regression cases around the CPU KV tile boundary:

* `KV = 63`, `64`, and `65`;
* `logit_softcap = 0` and `1`;
* `F32` and `F16` KV types;
* `nb = 65`, covering both a full Q tile and a Q tail.

The unmasked cases are important because a mask can overwrite the incorrect finite padding logits with `-INFINITY` and hide the bug.

Before the fix, these two cases consistently failed:

```text
KV=65, logit_softcap=1, type_KV=F32
KV=65, logit_softcap=1, type_KV=F16
```

Observed NMSE was approximately:

```text
0.0072 - 0.0075
```

compared with the allowed threshold:

```text
5e-4
```

After the fix:

```text
CPU targeted tests:  12/12 passed
CUDA targeted tests: 12/12 passed
```

CUDA code is unchanged. Running the same regression cases on CUDA provides a cross-check that the tests describe the intended Flash Attention semantics rather than CPU-specific output.

### Validation

Validation was performed locally on Windows at commit `b49650a`, with the local `HEAD` and remote `master` both at `b49650a`.

```text

CUDA backend tests:  16123/16123 passed
```

title: llama: add byte-oriented per-sequence state file API
body:
## Overview

#26640 serializes llama-server slot state into a byte stream, but the per-sequence file API accepts caller-owned data as `llama_token[]`.
This requires llama-server to pad the payload to a multiple of `sizeof(llama_token)` and pass it through the token-oriented API.
This PR adds a byte-oriented per-sequence file API and migrates llama-server to use it directly.

Related issue: #27942

## Additional information

### Changes

* add `llama_state_seq_save_file_data` / `llama_state_seq_load_file_data` for byte-oriented per-sequence state persistence
* introduce sequence-state file format v4 with explicit `TOKENS` and `DATA` payload types and byte-sized payload lengths
* make both save APIs write v4 while retaining v3 read compatibility
* keep the token load API restricted to token payloads, while the byte API can load both token and arbitrary byte payloads
* migrate llama-server slot persistence to the byte-oriented API
* use `raw_buffer` for serialized `server_tokens`
* remove token-width padding and reinterpretation as `llama_token *`

Existing v3 sequence-state files are treated as token payloads and remain readable.

title: server : support slot save/restore with media inputs
body:
## Overview

This PR adds support for **saving and restoring slots that contain media input**. Upstream stores the KV sequence state and a plain token list, but does not preserve the media positions and `mtmd_input_chunk` state required to reconstruct a media-containing slot, so saving such a slot is currently rejected with HTTP 501.

This PR uses `mtmd_input_chunk_save()` / `mtmd_input_chunk_load()` from #26645 and stores the complete `server_tokens` state - tokens, media start positions, and serialized media chunks - as a single versioned packed payload. The same format is used for both text-only and media-containing slots.

Because the packed payload can be larger than the slot's `n_ctx`, the restore path first queries the saved payload size through `llama_state_seq_load_file()` before allocating the restore buffer. After restore, the reconstructed media state can participate in the existing media matching / prefix reuse path.

Closes #25854

## Serialization format

Newly saved slots use the same packed `server_tokens` format for both text-only and media-containing slots.

```text
[LLAMA_TOKEN_NULL]
[version]
[n_tokens][tokens...]
[n_media][start_idx...]
(
  [chunk_size][serialized media chunk]
)...
[zero padding]
```

The current format version is `1`.

`n_tokens` and `n_media` are stored as element counts for their respective vectors. All media start indices are written first, followed by the serialized media chunks in the same order.

* A text-only slot has `n_media = 0`
* The byte stream is zero-padded with 0-3 trailing bytes so that it can be stored as whole `llama_token` words

## Backward compatibility

Slot files written before this PR contain a plain token list in the token payload.

The restore path distinguishes the formats as follows:

* starts with `LLAMA_TOKEN_NULL`: versioned packed `server_tokens` format
* otherwise: legacy plain token list

Therefore, **text-only slot files saved by older servers can still be restored after this PR**.

Newly saved text-only slots use the packed format as well, so restoring a new-format slot file on an older server is not supported.

## `server_tokens` serialization

This PR adds `server_tokens::serialize()` and `server_tokens::deserialize()`.

Internal reader / writer helpers handle scalar and vector fields. Media chunks are serialized through `mtmd_input_chunk_save()` and restored through `mtmd_input_chunk_load()`.

The packed state stores the token sequence, media start positions, and serialized media chunks. `deserialize()` validates the format and payload boundaries, reconstructs the media chunks, checks the supported media types (IMAGE and AUDIO), and validates trailing padding. After deserialization, `server_tokens::validate()` validates text token IDs against the current vocabulary and checks the mapping between media chunks and their token ranges.

An `mmproj` is required only when the restored state actually contains media.

## Slot save

`llama_state_seq_save_file()` returning `0` is handled as an error. The `n_saved` API field continues to report the **logical number of tokens held by the slot**, rather than the size of the packed representation.

## Slot restore

Serialized media chunks can make the packed payload larger than the slot's `n_ctx`.

This PR therefore allows `llama_state_seq_load_file()` to query the saved payload count when `tokens_out == nullptr`, without restoring the sequence state. The server uses that count to allocate the payload buffer before performing the actual load.

After deserialization, the logical token count is checked against the slot's `n_ctx` and the restored tokens are validated against the current model. If restore or validation fails, the slot is cleared before returning the error.

## Slot erase

Erase remains unsupported for slots containing media; its media gate is unchanged.

## Testing

Local validation:

* `test-mtmd-c-api` with assertions enabled: **passed**
* `test_slot_save.py` + `test_vision_api.py`: **28 passed**

Main API-level cases verified:

* text-only and image-containing slot save / restore
* restore of a legacy plain-token slot file
* multiple images
* same-image prefix reuse, including across a server restart
* no image-prefix reuse with a different image
* restoration of a packed payload larger than `n_ctx`
* graceful failure without an `mmproj`, leaving the slot usable

## Benchmark

Qwen3.5-2B Q8_0 + BF16 projector / RTX 4070 / Flash Attention (`-fa on`) / `--cache-ram 0`

3316-token multimodal prompt with a 3303-token reusable prefix, median of 3 runs:

* cold prompt processing: **292.38 ms**
* restore + same image prompt processing: **21.82 ms**
* prompt processing speedup: **13.4x**
* cold completion HTTP request: **298.77 ms**
* restore + same image completion HTTP request: **28.16 ms**
* completion HTTP speedup: **10.6x**
* restore API: **9.80 ms**
* saved state size: **60.9 MB**

With a different image, the restored image prefix was not reused.

## Additional information

* Media slot files are expected to be restored with the same model / `mmproj` configuration.
* Broader portability across server versions or endianness is not guaranteed.
* For SWA models, prefix reuse after restore requires `--swa-full`.
* A future sequence-state API for arbitrary raw user data could remove the current `llama_token`-width packing and padding workaround.

title: server: configurable prompt context checkpoints (LLAMA_CKPT_OFFSETS)
body:
## Overview

For every new prompt the server creates context checkpoints (by default: start of the last user message, `4 + n_ubatch` tokens before the end, and 4 tokens before the end). For recurrent / hybrid models each checkpoint copies the full recurrent state, and over RPC that copy crosses the network. On a two-node cluster serving Qwen3.8-27B (recurrent hybrid, ~21 recurrent layers on the RPC worker) each checkpoint costs ~66-69 MB over 1GbE (~0.6 s), and in multi-turn serving most of the default checkpoints are never used for reuse - so the traffic is mostly wasted.

This makes the checkpoint layout configurable:

- `LLAMA_CKPT_OFFSETS` - list of offsets from the end of the prompt (`"u"` = `4 + n_ubatch`), e.g. `LLAMA_CKPT_OFFSETS=4` keeps a single checkpoint
- `LLAMA_CKPT_LAST_USER=0` - drops the checkpoint at the start of the last user message

Unset = current behavior, byte for byte.

## Changes

- `common/speculative`: pass the target context to the draft contexts as `ctx_other`, so speculative (MTP) state is checkpointed/restored consistently with the target
- `server`: parse the two env vars and build the checkpoint offset list from them; default list unchanged

## Perf check

Two-node RPC cluster (RTX 4070 12GB controller + worker over 1GbE), Qwen3.8-27B UD-IQ3_S, KV q4_0, 64K context, 3 slots, MTP draft:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| network traffic per turn | ~287 MB | ~150 MB |
| short turn latency | 3.72 s | 2.47 s |
| new prompt latency | 5.23 s | 3.89 s |
| new session sharing a ~10.5K system prompt | 10466 tokens reprocessed, 17.1 s | 15 tokens reprocessed, 2.5 s |

Checkpoint reuse behavior unchanged (reprocessed-token counts identical to upstream). Solo decode unchanged (~48 tok/s).

## Additional information

Tested in production on the two-node cluster above: 3 concurrent sessions, multi-turn, MTP acceptance 35-71% after turn 1, no errors.

title: sycl : add a work-around for Level Zero crash/hang
body:
## Overview

There is a bug in Level Zero that will crash or hang llama.cpp when using p2p in tensor split mode. See intel/compute-runtime#995 issue.

To avoid the issue, a contiguous block of direct memory is used which ensures that both GPUs involved in the p2p operation map it as one.

This only affects the tensor-split all-reduce buffers.

Run with GGML_SYCL_COMM_DIRECT_ALLOC=1 to enable the work-around.

## Additional information

The crash itself is a Level Zero bug, but while the driver fix in intel/compute-runtime is pending, this will be a work around for that.

The issue is triggered with `-sm tensor` and SYCL, and happens when the GPUs have a different physical mapping. The owning GPU may see a contiguous range, but the accessing GPU may have gaps.

## Requirements

<!-- IMPORTANT: Please do NOT delete this section, otherwise your PR may be rejected -->

I asked Claude Opus to work around the bug in intel/compute-runtime by simply not using a buffer that can be mapped non-contiguously. By not using the pool, but directly allocating, we get contiguous blocks.

When contiguous (for both GPUs involved in the p2p copy) there will be no crash and no hang.

I told Claude to add an environment variable as gate, for lowest possible impact on existing behaviour.

I checked the code that was produced, made sure allocations and deallocations were correct. I also tested before/after behaviours.
